The Task Force on Definitions, Criteria, and Indicators for Interruption of Transmission and Elimination of Leprosy (TFCEL) was established to develop practical definitions, criteria, and milestones for assessing the interruption of transmission and elimination of leprosy as a disease. The Task Force met virtually on a monthly basis and held a final meeting at the Central Leprosy Teaching and Research Institute (CLTRI) in Chengalpattu, India, from March 24 to 26, 2021. The meeting aimed to agree on criteria for defining the interruption of transmission and elimination of leprosy, recommend a template for country dossiers, and propose a verification exercise. Dr. Erwin Cooreman, Team Leader of the Global Leprosy Programme (GLP), welcomed participants and explained the Task Force's objectives, which included drafting definitions for the interruption of transmission and elimination of leprosy, identifying criteria for different phases of leprosy control, and developing a framework for verification. The Task Force also referenced other diseases while developing these documents. Ms. Rekha Shukla, Joint Secretary of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India, delivered the inaugural address. She expressed gratitude to WHO for the opportunity to contribute to the issue and highlighted India's commitment to achieving a leprosy-free status. She emphasized the importance of moving beyond elimination as a public health problem to achieving the interruption of transmission and elimination of the disease. She noted the significant increase in the proposed budget for leprosy elimination and the Prime Minister's personal appeal for a Leprosy-Free India. She urged the application of different phases and indicators to define the interruption of transmission and elimination at sub-national levels. Dr. V.R.R. Pemmraju, Technical Officer of GLP, outlined the meeting's objectives, which included discussing and drafting the verification process for defining the interruption of transmission and elimination of leprosy. Specific objectives included reviewing documents developed by TFCEL, deciding on criteria for different phases and indicators, advising on a template for country dossiers, and validating criteria and tools with data from low-burden districts. Dr. Md. Jamsheed Ahmed, Regional Adviser for Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs), summarized the conclusions of an informal consultation held in Mexico City in February 2020. The consultation emphasized the need to build on past achievements and prepare for the interruption of transmission, as outlined in the NTD Roadmap 2021–2030. Key recommendations included mapping cases from the past five years, universal application of contact tracing and post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), and further research on the role of armadillos in leprosy's natural history. Criteria for interruption of transmission and zero incidence of disease should be consolidated and developed further, with a Task Force established to oversee this process. Dr. Erwin Cooreman explained the activities of TFCEL, which included defining criteria for countries to demonstrate progress toward interruption of transmission and elimination of leprosy. The Task Force developed draft definitions, criteria, and indicators for assessing readiness to move to the next phase of leprosy control. It also proposed a framework for verification, including a country dossier template and independent review mechanisms. Mr. John Kurian George, Country Coordinator for FAIRMED-India, presented findings from a three-year pilot project on the impact of migration among persons affected by leprosy. Migration is a significant obstacle to leprosy elimination, as there is no focused program to manage leprosy patients who migrate. The project, conducted in Bihar, Chandigarh, Delhi, and Uttar Pradesh, aims to understand migration patterns and their impact on treatment and health-seeking behavior. The project focuses on bringing stakeholders together, understanding migration among leprosy patients, and providing recommendations for leprosy programs. The expected outcome is evidence-based recommendations for leprosy management policies and programs that are acceptable to stakeholders and partners in India's leprosy ecosystem.
